status.comment: standalone CLI contracts: roots, preconditions, effects, exit codes and idempotency

facts.CLI-INVOCATION: Invocation is the installed `bin/codkit` or `bin/codkit.ps1` from any cwd. `npm run codkit -- …` is allowed only as a developer entry from toolRoot; the patch set carries no copy of the runtime.
facts.CLI-PRINTS-ROOT-SOURCES: A command that uses the patch set prints `patches: /abs/path (source: flag|env|settings)`; a command that uses the tree also prints `fork tree: /abs/path (source: flag|env|settings)`. Under `--json` all three roots live only in the top-level `roots.tool|patches|fork` of schema 2; the command `data` may repeat the subject of the answer, but it does not replace `roots`.
facts.CLI-GLOBAL-FLAGS: Global flags: `--patches-dir <path>`, `--fork-dir <path>`, `--json`, `--ci`, `--verbose`. Both path flags take part in an independent flag → env → settings precedence.
facts.CLI-EXIT-CODES: Exit codes: `0` success; `1` a check did not pass (markers, inventory, the delta did not apply, a red test, a guard); `2` a startup/environment error (no git-lfs, an unreachable pin, no permissions, a broken config); `3` the cycle has to stop (a human is needed: a conflict, a design decision). An internal error (a bug) is 2 as well, with a request to attach the `--verbose` log.
facts.CLI-NON-INTERACTIVE: The main path is non-interactive; there are no stdin questions. Every error prints a `hint:` - what to do (PROP-012 §2).
facts.CLI-IDEMPOTENCY: Running any command again after it completed successfully is a no-op or the same result (the exceptions are stated). An interruption (SIGINT/kill) leaves no partially applied state that the next command would not recognize: every command begins by validating the actual state, not a cache.

p.CMD-WHERE: Print toolRoot and the independently resolved patchesDir/forkDir with their source and exists. Neither external directory has to exist or to be configured; `where` does not read `codkit.json` and has no side effects. `data`: `{patches: null|{path,source,exists}, fork: null|{path,source,exists}}`; the top-level `roots` holds the same roots plus tool. Codes: 0, except for broken settings or a disjoint-roots violation - 2.

p.CMD-CHECK-TREE: The identity/fitness check (PROP-008 §2) without changes. The `--require-clean` flag demands cleanliness (dirt → 1). The output is a table of `ok|fail` checks plus the first error with its hint. Codes: 0 fit; 1 unfit but repairable with codkit commands (the wrong pin, for instance - hint "run codkit load"); 2 fatally unfit (not a git repository, not upstream, no lfs).

p.CMD-CLONE: Clone the tree into an empty/absent directory and check out the pin. **Local only**: under `--ci` it is an immediate exit 2 `CK-E-NET-FORBIDDEN`. Preconditions: the path is resolved; the directory is absent or empty; a source is given - `publishRemoteUrl` from the config or `--from <url>`. Steps: `git clone --no-checkout <url> <path>`; `git checkout --detach <pin.sha>`; when there are LFS paths - `git lfs install --local` and `git lfs pull` (the network is allowed - the command is a local one); a final `check-tree`. Idempotency: a non-empty directory with a fit tree → the message "already present", exit 0; non-empty with foreign content → 2. Cloning happens only through this command or through an explicit `load --clone-if-missing` (never as a side effect: a typo in a path must not start a download of gigabytes).

p.SHALLOW-CLONE-DROPPED: **Shallow cloning is dropped** (the M0 implementation): the anchored origin check `##ID-CHECK-ORIGIN` requires the root commit of the history to be reachable, and a shallow tree does not have it by construction - "shallow is admissible as long as the pin is reachable" from an early edition did not survive implementation: such a tree would fail `CK-E-NOT-UPSTREAM` forever, on every command. If a cheaper clone is ever needed, that is a separate decision with a different origin-check scheme.

cmd-sync.title: 5. codkit load […] and the two-way codkit sync […]

p.CMD-SYNC: A tombstone (Phase 1 of the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign, 2026-09-06): the one-way `sync` command was renamed to `load`, and its contract moved to the `CMD-LOAD` anchor of this section. The anchor itself is neither renamed nor deleted - the address of a cited anchor never changes (NEVER-RENAME-OR-DELETE-A-CITED-ANCHOR). The second life of the name: since Phase 8 of that campaign (2026-09-06, decision D15) `codkit sync` is a real two-way command, and the live contract is `CMD-SYNC-TWO-WAY` below. Between Phase 1 and Phase 8 the name was a stub that exited 2 ("renamed to codkit load"), so that scripts carrying the old meaning would break loudly; an alias is deliberately refused now as well.

p.CMD-SYNC-TWO-WAY: **The two-way command** (Phase 8 of the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign, decisions D15/D16/D19/D20; the algorithm is PROP-008 §5a). `codkit sync [--squash] [--commit] [--message m] [--discard] [--fresh] [--dry-run] [--abort] [--continue]`: one command that extracts the work of the tree (as `save` does, replay of commits and `--squash` included) and delivers the patchset shift (as `load` does), by rule D16 for each file: the tree only → extract; patchset only → apply the patchset version, and overwriting the target during the rebuild is explained; both sides → **a diff3 materialization** (Phase 8b, D19): the 3-way merge is laid down as markers inside the tree file under a live transaction, exit 1 `CK-E-BOTH-SIDES-EDITED` with the list of files and both roads - a human resolves the markers (as in the resolve phase of the cycle), then `codkit sync --continue` finishes the run and `codkit sync --abort` returns everything to how it was (PROP-008 `##SYNC-CONFLICT-DIFF3`, `##SYNC-ABORT`, `##SYNC-CONTINUE`); there is no automatic merge. An own conflict on both sides stays the "choose a side" recipe (own code has no marker blocks), and under `--discard` so does the uncommitted both-sides part - `--continue` is extraction, not discarding. The D17 lineage is checked as in `save`: not an ancestor of the patchset HEAD → `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED`; a mark without an artifact map → the same refusal with the hint "run codkit load once" (R13). Order: the tree lock → a live transaction → `CK-E-SYNC-IN-PROGRESS` → check-tree/ref-preflight → D8 → D17 → classification → both sides → a refusal **before the first write** (no transaction file, no moved ref, not a byte) → `--dry-run` (print the classification, exit 0, nothing written) → write the transaction → the save half → the rebuild = the load half → the consumed ref → the mark → lift the transaction. `--discard` means the same as it does for `load` (D11): tree commits are discarded on purpose (a consumed ref), while the guard goes on guarding edits; under `--ci` it is exit 2. Nothing moved on either side and there is no transaction → the answer of the load engine, usually "up to date", exit 0, without a transaction. `--abort`/`--continue` are the recovery of a stopped synchronization (Phase 8b, D21): no record - an honest exit 2; the extraction flags (`--squash`/`--commit`/`--message`/`--fresh`) apply to `--continue`, while `--discard`/`--dry-run`, and any flag at all with `--abort`, are exit 2. Codes: 0; 1 (`CK-E-BOTH-SIDES-EDITED` - materialized unresolved markers, "the merge never reached the file" and an own conflict; `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED`; `CK-E-SYNC-IN-PROGRESS` - a live record and the refusals of `--abort` over someone else's work; the inheritance from `save`: markers/Cause/a forbidden target/a deletion); 2 (the environment, `--ci`+`--discard`, a recovery with no record or with foreign flags).

p.CMD-LOAD: Bring the tree to the pin and apply the delta (the algorithm is PROP-008 §3). Preconditions: the config is valid; the tree passes `check-tree`; the generated branch is not shared with a sibling worktree (`CK-E-WORKTREE-REF-SHARED`, exit 2 - the preflight runs BEFORE the dirt check, ruling D7 of 2026-09-06); **there are no unextracted edits and no tree commits** (the guard of PROP-008 §4: edits are exit 1 `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE` with the list of files and the hint "run codkit save, or codkit status; codkit load --discard drops tree commits deliberately"; tree commits are the same code, "N commit(s) in the fork tree since the last codkit apply are not in patchset yet"; HEAD off the branch while foreign commits exist is `CK-E-TREE-HEAD`, exit 1). `--fresh` is the "from scratch" mode: a reset to the pin plus a cleanup of untracked paths by the whitelist before the delta is applied (PROP-011 §4); a known materialization of overlay targets is replaced by the same run (PROP-005 §5 `##OVERLAY-KNOWN-MATERIALIZATION`, PROP-008 §4). `--dry-run` is a forecast: the full apply cycle in memory/index without changing working files or refs; it prints classified outcomes (the report format is the one `cycle` uses); `forecast` uses it. `--discard` (decision D11, Phase 6 of the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign) sacrifices the third half of the guard **by name**: tree commits above the last generated tip are discarded on purpose, by the very mechanism the guard used to keep from being used blindly - an ordinary rebuild of the branch (the commits stop being reachable from HEAD) plus the consumed ref `refs/codkit/consumed/…` (PROP-006 §1 `##CONSUMED-REFS`, which only `gc` cleans) and the message `discarded N commit(s): <first>..<last>; kept as <ref>`. The ref is written **before** the rebuild, under the lock of the shared repository, right after the precondition "the foreign set has not changed since the check, otherwise `CK-E-INTERNAL` before any ref or file moves": unlike `save`, the patch set has replayed nothing here, and the ref is the only keeper of the line (the parent session's ruling of 2026-09-06: a crash between the ref and the rebuild leaves the ref on commits that are still alive - "a discard begun and not finished", which loses nothing and names itself; `save` has the reverse order - there the patch set is the keeper already). The bounds of the flag: the guard goes on guarding file edits and own code (mixed dirt is an ordinary refusal), and the anomaly of a rewritten history and HEAD off the branch as well (`CK-E-TREE-HEAD`); without tree commits it is a no-op, exit 0 with an info line; under `--ci` it is exit 2 `CK-E-CONFIG`: a non-interactive run does not decide on its own to throw away someone else's work. Side effects (not under dry-run): the branch `codkit/applied/<pin.tag>` is recreated (when the fingerprint changed), the tree HEAD is on its tip, own code is copied, `product.overrides.json` is written, the effective `info/exclude` is restored, and the mark and the cache are updated. A repeat with no changes is a fast no-op (the comparison rule of PROP-006 §1) that prints `up to date`. Codes: 0; 1 (the guard; an artifact did not apply - on its own pin that means a broken artifact `CK-E-ARTIFACT-BROKEN`, and which one is printed); 2 (the environment). The former name: between Phase 1 and Phase 8 of the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign `codkit sync` was a usage error without an envelope (exit 2, "renamed to codkit load"), so that scripts carrying the old meaning would break loudly; since Phase 8 the name belongs to the two-way command - `##CMD-SYNC-TWO-WAY` above.

p.CMD-LOAD-DISCARD-WORKTREE: **The extension of `--discard` (decision D-S3-5, confirmed by the owner on 2026-09-08, option 2):** only together with `--fresh` does the `--discard` flag drop, besides tree commits, the working-tree edits of **tracked upstream files without marker blocks** (today `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE`, a manual `git checkout` in the managed tree): the plan prints every such path as a `discard <path>` line before the first write, the actual discarding matches the plan one for one (R14), and the file returns to the pin plus the delta. Never discarded: files with marker blocks (an unextracted intervention may live there - `save` is for it; such a file stays a `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE` refusal even with `--discard`), own code and own extensions (their side of the truth is `save`/`load` per PROP-008), and untracked files outside the cleanup lists. Without `--fresh` the `--discard` flag still touches tree commits only. The reason: a build of the tree rewrites a tracked file with a build artifact that is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a human edit, and returning to dev mode must not require a git command typed by hand in a managed tree. Rejected: a separate flag (a second name for the same "sacrifice by name" gesture), and a list of the known side effects of a build (it cannot be kept current across pins). The norm of the release protocol: packaging preferably runs in a throwaway clone, as `publish` does, so that the dev tree receives no build artifacts.

p.CMD-STATUS: Print: the pin; the tip of the branch; tree commits outside patchset - the line `tree commits not in patchset: N` plus up to 20 `<short> <subject>` lines (`data.treeCommits: {base, count, commits}`); with N>0 the `reload needed …` line is NOT printed - moving to patchset is exactly what would destroy those commits, and the question is addressed to `save`; the currency of the branch (up to date / reload needed) is printed when N=0; **the line `loaded from patchset commit: <sha|dirty|none|unknown>`** and, when the delta has shifted away from the mark, **`patchset moved since load: N artifact(s)`** with the list (the data of the manual `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED` recipe; `data.loadedFrom`, `data.patchsetMoved`; the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign, decision D10, Phase 7); own code - N changed files (the tree against `delta/own/`); own extensions - the line `own extensions: D declared, P path(s) differ between tree and patchset` with the list (PROP-005 `OWN-EXTENSION-UNIT`; `data.ownExtensions: {declared, differing}`), and their `extensions/<name>/` directories in the tree are own, not upstream dirt; **a stranded materialization** - an untracked `extensions/<name>/` directory of the tree that no declaration covers and that does not exist on the pin (the declaration was withdrawn, and a `load` without `--fresh` does not touch the directory - PROP-005 `OWN-EXTENSION-STRANDED`): the line `own extensions: … , S stranded materialization(s)` with the list of paths and the hint `codkit load --fresh removes it`; `data.ownExtensions.stranded: [path…]`; exit code 1 (there is something to remove); upstream files - M changed (dirt against HEAD, outside the own directory and outside the declared extensions), K marker blocks in them, the validity of the markers (pairing/id); uncommitted `delta/` changes in patchset while the tree is clean (a divergence in the direction of truth). Read-only; it works even while the lock is held. Codes: 0 clean/consistent; 1 there is something unextracted (edits, own code or tree commits) or the markers are invalid (an informational command - code 1 makes it usable in scripts). Time: seconds on a full tree.

p.STATUS-ADVICE-FOLLOWS-THE-LAYER: **The next step `status` prints follows the layer that owns the changed file, not the count of changed files.** A tree whose only difference from the pin is a **materialized overlay target** was told to `run codkit save`, which is wrong twice: `save` is about patch targets and an overlay target is not one, and the tool already knows the right recipe and prints it elsewhere (`load --fresh`, `spec://codkit/modules/codkit/PROP-005#OVERLAY-KNOWN-MATERIALIZATION`). `status` therefore classifies its changed upstream files the way the drift guard of `load --fresh` does - bytes exactly equal to the strict composition of the configured overlays over the clean pin file are codkit's own packaging state - reports them in `data.upstream.materializedOverlayTargets`, and when they are the ONLY thing the tree carries, names them and sends the reader to `codkit load --fresh`, saying which commands leave that state behind (`overlay apply`, `codkit package --keep-overlay`). One real edit beside them brings the `save` advice back: the recipe is only right while nothing else is there. The classification is read-only and never fatal - an unreadable pin or a broken overlay artifact costs the hint and nothing else - and the exit code is unchanged: there is still something to do, so it is still 1. Measured on 2026-09-09 by a consumer reading a colleague's log. **The second layer with a recipe of its own is the packaging residue**: a changed upstream file matching `build.packageScratch` of the type is not somebody's work either but a file the packager rewrote in passing, and `save` would carry a bumped version or a build flag into the delta. Such files are reported in `data.upstream.packagingScratch`, and while they are all the tree carries the line names them and sends the reader to `codkit load --fresh --discard` - the discard, because those bytes are a real edit of a tracked file and nothing else gives them up - adds that `codkit package` returns them itself unless the run was interrupted, and still names `save` for the reader who wrote the file themselves (`spec://codkit/modules/codkit/PROP-016#TYPE-PACKAGE-SCRATCH`).

p.CMD-SAVE: Extract the work (the algorithm is PROP-008 §4). Without arguments it takes every changed file; with paths it is targeted. Work = the resulting state of the tree relative to the last applied tip - committed and uncommitted together, tree commits included (PROP-008 §4 `##SAVE-CONSUMES-TREE-COMMITS`). **Tree commits are replayed one by one by default** (PROP-008 §4 `##SAVE-REPLAYS-TREE-COMMITS`): every foreign commit becomes a separate patchset commit with the original message, author and date plus the trailer `Codkit-Tree-Commit: <sha40>`; the person running the command commits, with their own identity. The analogy of the merge buttons of a pull request: the default is "rebase and merge", `--squash` is "squash and merge" (one commit `codkit save: squash of N tree commit(s)` listing `sha subject` in its body and carrying a trailer for every folded sha; `--message` supplies its subject); there is no analogue of "merge commit" by construction - the two histories live in two repositories, and there is no place for a third button. The uncommitted remainder lands in the working tree of patchset and is not committed; `--commit` commits it as a separate commit `codkit save: <N> file(s)` (`--message` is for that commit only). A state that changes no artifact is skipped with a message - a visible one, not silence. Idempotency: a patchset commit with the trailer `Codkit-Tree-Commit: <sha>` means "this state is replayed already" - a repeated `save` (after an interruption, for instance) skips it, while `--squash` plays out the rest in one commit; a `save` with no changed files AND no tree commits is a no-op (exit 0, "nothing to save"); a `--squash` with no tree commits is a no-op as well, with a message that there is nothing to fold. Steps: mirroring own code (tree→patchset), validating the edits, regenerating the patches file by file, rebuilding the branch without touching files, the report. A targeted `save <paths>` does not touch the branch while tree commits exist, and says that the commits stay until a full save (`##SAVE-SCOPED-BRANCH-RULE`). **The patchset shift** (the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign, decisions D17/D18, Phase 7): before any write, `save` checks that patchset has not moved under the tree since the last load - an edited artifact or a `git switch` to another branch → exit 1 `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED`, nothing written (no artifact, no own byte, no commit, the ref untouched), the text carrying the sha of the load, the list of shifted artifacts and the manual recipe (PROP-008 §4 `##PATCHSET-MOVED-RULE`, `##LINEAGE-CHECK`; the recipe is in the FAQ as well); a patchset that was dirty at the moment of the load is a warning and the run continues. Codes: 0; 1 (an edit outside the markers - including one in an intermediate commit, named with the sha/subject of that commit - a forbidden target, the deletion of an upstream file, a malformed `Cause:` in the message of a tree commit, HEAD off the branch while foreign commits exist - `CK-E-TREE-HEAD` - the patchset shift - `CK-E-PATCHSET-MOVED` - with the exact files/lines and a hint); 2.

p.SAVE-SCOPED-BRANCH-RULE: Clarifications from the M0 implementation: a targeted `save <paths>` does NOT rebuild the branch while changes remain OUTSIDE the paths (a rebuild would wipe out unextracted work) - it prints a warning, and a full `save` completes the branch; a `--commit` on a delta that already matches the last commit is "nothing to commit", exit 0; an own edit on the patchset side alone extracts nothing (the next `load` delivers the patchset version).

p.SAVE-EXTRACTS-TWO-LAYERS: `save` extracts TWO layers: patch and own (and under `--commit` it stages only their paths). The overlay/resource/removed/rule layers are authored by hand on the patchset side and committed with ordinary commits; `load` delivers them into the tree (materialization). The lesson of the M1 polygon: editing a resource target in the tree leads `save` to an honest `CK-E-HEADER-MISSING` (the file changed, there is no patch) - the resource procedure is to place the artifact in `delta/resources/` by hand and then run `load`. The defect "the first `save` after a hand-written resource artifact tripped over its own guard" is FIXED in M1: the guard "nothing must move" tolerates overwrites explained by artifacts of the non-patch layers of the materializable plan (they are printed as info), and it still raises `CK-E-INTERNAL` on unexplained ones. A target described by a patch and by a resource at once falls among the "explained" ones - that is an authoring error of the delta (two artifacts for one file), and it has no guard of its own.

cmd-marker-new.title: 8. codkit marker new file --id CK-… --type t --owner o --reason text [--category c] [--layer patch|entry-module] [--line n]

p.CMD-MARKER-NEW: Scaffold a marker block: it inserts a pair of markers in the form that matches the file's extension at the `--line` line (or at the end of the file). Required flags: `--id`, `--type`, `--owner`, `--reason`; `--category` defaults to `follow`; `--layer` is `patch|entry-module` and defaults to `patch` (`rewrite-rule` is reserved for the rule generator and is forbidden here). The file is edited in the tree only; `save` then creates the patch. Checks: the id is unique (against the existing patches, the drafts and the blocks of the target file; once the inventory exists, against it too), and the file is an upstream one (not own, not a forbidden target). Idempotency: a repeat with the same id is a refusal, 1, "id already used". `--add-block` (see `CMD-MARKER-NEW-ADD-BLOCK`) is a second block of the same intervention in the same file. Codes (the M0 clarification): wrong usage (a flag value outside the lists of the conventions) → 2 `CK-E-CONFIG`; the state of the tree or of the delta (a forbidden target, a taken id, an unknown owner, a malformed id) → 1.

p.CMD-MARKER-NEW-ADD-BLOCK: `codkit marker new <file> --id <id> --add-block [--line <n>]` is one more marker block of an intervention the file already carries (PROP-004 `MR-SEVERAL-BLOCKS-ONE-ID`: a graft is an import and a call site). Conditions: the id belongs to this file - its header stands in the file's patch artifact or in its pending draft (otherwise 1 `CK-E-MARKER-DUP-ID`, "is not the intervention of"); the file already contains a block with that id (otherwise 1 `CK-E-MARKER-ARTIFACT-MISMATCH`, "carries no block … yet", with the hint `codkit load`); the header flags (`--type`, `--owner`, `--reason`, `--category`, `--layer`) are forbidden together with `--add-block` - 2 `CK-E-CONFIG`: an intervention has one header. The draft is neither written nor changed; `save` gathers every block of the id into one patch. `--json`: `data: {target, id, line, block: 'added'}`.

p.PENDING-HEADER-MECHANISM: **The header draft** (an implementation decision of M0 that closes the gap "marker new printed the header into nowhere"): `marker new` writes the header fields of the future patch into `.codkit/pending/<enc(target)>.json` (`{id,layer,type,category,owner,reason,link:"none"}`), where `layer` is always present and holds either the explicit value or the `patch` default; one target is reserved by exactly one draft or by an existing `.ckpatch`, a second `marker new` with a different id is rejected **before** the tree is changed and never overwrites the draft, while an exact repeat of the same unfinished operation idempotently completes the "marker + draft" pair; `save`, when it creates a NEW patch, takes the header from here and removes the draft; an existing patch keeps its own header byte for byte. Neither an existing patch nor a draft for a new target file → exit 1 `CK-E-HEADER-MISSING` with the hint "run codkit marker new <file> --id … first". The drafts are local (`.codkit/` is not committed) - the metadata reaches git only inside a `.ckpatch`.

p.CMD-RERESOLVE: A 3-way application of an old hunk onto the current tree file (scenario R1: a conflict of two branches over one patch file is resolved by a replay, `common/PROP-002` `##CONFLICT-RESOLVED-BY-REPLAY`). Precondition: an "old" patch exists. Its source is chosen as strictly the first existing option in this order: (1) the path from an explicit `--patch`; (2) the adjacent `<patch-path>.orig` left by a merge tool; (3) the blob `git show HEAD:<patch-path>` while the merge is still under way (`MERGE_HEAD` exists and `HEAD` is the feature tip before the merge); (4) the blob `git show HEAD^1:<patch-path>` from an already created two-parent merge commit whose first parent is the feature before the merge. `MERGE_HEAD` is not a source of the old feature patch. If no source exists, exit 1 with the list of the sources that were checked and a hint to pass `--patch`. The algorithm: base = the file at the pin; ours = the current file in the tree (already carrying the version of the target branch); theirs = base + the old patch; `git merge-file` (PROP-008 §5). Clean → the file in the tree is updated and it prints "resolved, run codkit save"; a conflict → the standard conflict markers are left in the tree file, exit 1, hint "edit conflicts in IDE, then codkit save".

p.CMD-INVENTORY: Generate the inventory (PROP-006 §3–4) into `.codkit/out/inventory.json` (and `.md` under `--md`); print a summary of the metrics. `--diff <ref>`: build the inventory for the patchset state at `<ref>` as well (reading the artifacts through `git show <ref>:<path>` without a checkout) and print the diff: added/removed/changed entries plus the delta of the metrics; the format is a table by id. Codes: 0; 1 - the inventory was built, but there are consistency violations (the same checks `verify` makes, in reporting mode); 2.

p.CMD-VERIFY: Every integrity check without a build (the PR threshold; seconds): the markers are valid; every hunk of every patch is inside the markers; the "marker ↔ artifact" consistency holds in both directions; the ids are unique; the owner exists; the config-overlay/resource-file layers and the hide category have a guard test; for rules, `expectedMatches` agrees; for overlays, `expectUpstream` agrees; own files are covered by units; the removed registry is covered by guard tests; "there are no interventions outside the inventory"; `forbiddenServiceIds` do not overlap. It requires the tree (for the checks against the pin it uses the git objects of the tree and does not read the working files - it works on a dirty tree as well). Codes: 0; 1 (any violation; each on a line of its own, `code: file:line: text + hint`); 2.

p.CMD-OVERLAY: `check`: for an overlay target - schema validation, `expectUpstream` against the pin, and (when the target is materialized in the tree) the comparison "the current content = the pin + the operations". `apply`: materialization by option 2 (PROP-005 §5) - overwriting the target file in the tree. An ordinary developer does not need it (`load` covers the dev channel); packaging, `publish` and `ci` use it. Codes: 0; 1 (`CK-E-OVERLAY-DRIFT` - apply refuses on drift as well: an intervention whose upstream expectation is broken must not be materialized); 2. A note (M1, REPAIR-005): `overlay apply` on a developer's tree makes the next ordinary `load` red with `CK-E-DIRTY-TREE` - which is right by the model (apply is a packaging operation; an ordinary `load` cannot withdraw its own bytes silently: the fast path would answer "up to date" and leave the packaging bytes standing). The way back to dev mode is `codkit load --fresh`: before refusing, the guard classifies every tracked overlay target that differs from HEAD, and only bytes exactly equal to the strict composition of the configured overlays count as a known codkit materialization that the run replaces (PROP-005 §5 `##OVERLAY-KNOWN-MATERIALIZATION`); any extra, missing or hand-made byte stays dirt. A direct `git checkout` of the target is not needed.

p.CMD-OVERLAY-CHECK-TREE: **What `check` calls a materialized target** - the tree side of `##CMD-OVERLAY`, which compares the file with "the pin + the operations" only when the target is materialized. The target counts as materialized when its **content** differs from the pin's blob, and the content of a file is what git stores for it at its path: git's own hash of the file under the tree's attributes (`git hash-object -- <target>` in codkit's isolated configuration, PROP-002 `##GIT-ENV-ISOLATION`), not its raw bytes. A file that differs from the pin's blob only by git's working-copy conversion is the pin's file, because git itself calls it unchanged: the CRLF line endings a checkout on Windows writes for a `text=auto` file of upstream - which is what a `git checkout -- <target>` there leaves behind - are not an edit. On such a tree, and on one that has no such file at all, the target is **not materialized**: `check` does not compare it with the operations and does not report `CK-E-OVERLAY-DRIFT` over it; it says so in its own line (`<target>: N overlay(s) agree with the pin; the target is not materialized in the fork tree …`) and in its own status, `data.inTree: "pin"` or `"absent"` with `matchesOperations: null`, and exits 0. The codes of `##CMD-OVERLAY` stay 0, 1 and 2: a target that is not materialized is a check that passed, and it is the everyday state of a development tree, whose `product.json` stays the pin's while `load` writes the dev channel. A materialized target (`data.inTree: "materialized"`, `materialized: true`) is compared byte for byte with the strict composition of PROP-005 `##OVERLAY-KNOWN-MATERIALIZATION`: equal bytes are `matchesOperations: true` and exit 0; any other bytes - a hand edit of the pin's file or of a materialization, a stale materialization, a converted copy of one - are `CK-E-OVERLAY-DRIFT`, exit 1, `matchesOperations: false`. `apply` reports the same three fields for the file as it found it.

p.CMD-OVERLAY-NEW: `codkit overlay new <target> --id CK-… --type t --owner o --reason text [--category c] --contract-test <id>…` scaffolds the artifact of this layer, the way `marker new` scaffolds a patch and `gen feature` an own unit. It exists because writing one by hand was a refusal by construction: the metadata has to be canonical JSON in the **schema's key order**, and `CK-E-ARTIFACT-BROKEN: metadata bytes are not canonical JSON` names the rules - key order, two-space indentation, UTF-8 without BOM, LF, one final LF - without naming the order, which lives in the serializer. Every first overlay of every patch set therefore cost one refusal that taught nothing. The command writes `delta/overlays/<target with / as __>.overlay.json`: the canonical metadata, the pin of `codkit.json` as `<tag>@<sha>`, `link` and `cause` as the literal `none`, the guard tests of `--contract-test`, and an **empty** list of operations for the author to fill in. `--contract-test` is repeatable and required - a guard test is mandatory for this layer (PROP-005 §5), because the overlay leaves no marker in the target file and the test is the only thing that fails when upstream takes the key away - and there is no `--layer`: the artifact IS the layer. The metadata is held to the same vocabularies `marker new` holds an intervention to (the id pattern, the intervention types, the categories, an owner of `delta/owners.json`), the id must be free among the overlays of the delta, and an existing artifact of the target is never overwritten. A target the project type does not declare is a warning and not a refusal - the layer already restricts an undeclared target to the strictest keys the type states (PROP-005 `##OVERLAY-NON-PRODUCT-TARGETS`) - and no fork tree is touched or needed: the target is a path in the tree, not a file this command reads. Codes: 0; 1 - the state of the delta (`CK-E-MARKER-BAD-ID`, `CK-E-MARKER-DUP-ID`, `CK-E-OWNER-UNKNOWN`, `CK-E-GEN-EXISTS`); 2 - what was typed or the configuration (`CK-E-CONFIG`). `--json`: `data: {artifact, target, id, type, category, owner, reason, pin, contractTests, operations: 0}`.

p.CMD-BUILD: A wrapper over the watch daemons (PROP-010 §2). Channels: `transpile`, `typecheck`, `extensions`, `copilot` for the `vscode` type, `typecheck` and `bundle` for `theia`, whatever the patch set declared for `generic`; `--channel all` is all of them. **The default of `up` - and of the one pass of `ci --profile build` - is the type's own answer** (`build.defaultChannels`, `spec://codkit/modules/codkit/PROP-016#TYPE-BUILD-CHANNELS`) and not a pair of names the engine carries: the pair `transpile,typecheck` was a module constant until a family whose channels are `typecheck` and `bundle` met it, and that family's build profile therefore never bundled its application. A name the profile does not declare is ignored, and a type that names none has every declared channel as its default, so the bare form of the command is never a refusal over a name from another family (clarified on 2026-09-09 with the `theia` type, corrected the same day when the constant was found in the ci engine as well). `up` starts the missing daemons in the background (detached, logs in `.codkit/build/<channel>.log`) and does not wait for the end of a pass; `down` stops them (by the process tree); `status` reports living/dead per channel (by probing the command line of the process, not by a pid file); `errors` waits for the end of the current pass and prints the errors of the last finished pass in full (`--mine` narrows it to files from the inventory and own code). The rule (in our own words from the clean-room rewriting): running the compiler over the whole project directly is forbidden - the daemons carry the compilation; `errors` is called once and its output is read in full. The codes of `errors`: 0 there are no errors; 1 there are errors; 2 the daemon is not running AND there is no finished pass in the log (hint "codkit build up"); a dead daemon with a FINISHED pass in the log gives the result of that pass (0/1) plus a warning (useful for a single CI pass; the M1 clarification). The bounds of the post-mortem view (the M1 implementation): a pass from the log is given out only when a daemon record EXISTS (the record ties the log to a particular start and a particular tree; `up` rotates the log exactly when it creates the record) - a channel without a record was either never started or was stopped by `build down`, which retires the channel together with its answer; the LAST FINISHED pass is what is given out (a daemon that died inside a new pass gives out the previous finished one); without `--channel` the channels that have an answer are listed (the living ones and the dead ones with a pass). The codes of the other subcommands (the M1 clarification): `up` - 0 started or already living, 1 a refusal (a foreign watcher, no script, a channel of another tree, a concurrent start), 2 the tree is unfit; `down`/`status` - always 0. The spelling of "all channels" is `--channel all` (one single form). Dedicated `CK-E-*` codes for these refusals are deliberately not created until their machine consumer (the skill of the cycle, M2) appears.

p.CMD-BUILD-EXITS-REPAIR009: REPAIR-009 clarifies the semantics without changing the codes: `build status` stays report-only and its exit 0 means that the OBSERVATION succeeded, not that every daemon is healthy - `starting` and `unknown` stay visible states in the line and in the JSON, and this is said explicitly in the reference and JSON documentation. `up` and `down` hold a contained per-channel operation lock (PROP-010 ##DAEMON-CHANNEL-LOCK) from the first probe to the final publication or the exact retirement; a competitor that loses returns a refusal without touching either the record or the process. `status`, `down` and `errors` are bound to the current tree: a record of another tree is shown honestly, `down` sends no signals, `errors` does not certify a foreign log, and a mutating or certifying mismatch is an environment code.

cmd-cycle.title: 14. codkit cycle start tag|sha / continue / status / restart [--yes] [--ci]

p.CMD-CYCLE: The orchestrator of the upgrade (PROP-009). `start` - preconditions: there is no active cycle (no `cycle/state.json`), the working tree of patchset is clean, and the target pin is reachable in the tree (otherwise 2 with a hint saying which fetch to run - there is no network); it creates the cycle branch and the pin commit, and starts the apply phase. `continue` - after a manual or agent resolution: it re-reads the state, extracts the resolutions that remain (a `save` of the affected files) and carries on through the phases. `status` - print the phase, the outcome counters and `nextAction`. `restart` - a reset to the beginning of the cycle: `git reset --hard` of the cycle branch to the parent of the pin commit plus the removal of `cycle/state.json` (confirmed by the `--yes` flag; under `--ci` only with `--yes`). `--ci` is the non-interactive keep-alive mode: the stopping points do not wait but end the process with code 3 and a full report. Codes: 0 the phase or the cycle is finished; 1 checks; 2 the environment; 3 a stop for a human.

p.CMD-FORECAST: A dry run of applying the delta onto an upstream ref. The choice is deterministic: the explicit `--ref <ref>`, otherwise exactly `refs/remotes/upstream/main`; searching for "the freshest" among similar refs, and a fallback to `origin/main`, are forbidden. The chosen name is resolved once through `git rev-parse --verify '<ref>^{commit}'` into a full SHA, and that SHA is printed and used by the whole run; a missing ref → exit 2 with a hint to pass `--ref` or to update the mirror beforehand. Under the global `--ci` the `--ref` flag is required, and its absence → exit 2 before the tree is read or changed. The implementation: the same apply engine in dry-run mode against the resolved SHA instead of the pin. The output is a report by owner: for every artifact whose outcome is worse than `clean` - the id, the owner, the outcome and the cause. There is no network: the freshness of the ref is the duty of CI (the mirror bot). Codes: 0 everything is clean; 1 there are future breakages (the "informational redness" of a nightly job); 2.

p.CMD-REBASE-ONTO-PIN: Rebinding the patches of a patchset feature branch to the pin of the target branch after an ordinary merge (guard R2b). The command does not guess `main` by name and does not use the merged `HEAD` as a source of feature patches.

facts.REBASE-TWO-PARENT-CONTRACT: `HEAD` must be a merge commit with exactly two parents: `HEAD^1` is the feature tip before the merge, `HEAD^2` is the merged-in target branch. A non-merge, an octopus merge, an unfinished merge and swapped parent roles are rejected with code 2 and a hint to repeat `git merge <target>` on the feature branch. The target pin is taken only from `codkit.json` at `HEAD^2`; the pin in the merged `HEAD` must match it. The source pin is taken from `codkit.json` at `HEAD^1`; both full SHAs must be reachable in the tree.
facts.REBASE-FEATURE-PATCH-SET: `M = git merge-base HEAD^1 HEAD^2` is computed. The transferable set is the `delta/patches/*.ckpatch` files existing at `HEAD^1` whose paths appear in `git diff --name-status M..HEAD^1 -- delta/patches/`; the blob of every patch is read strictly from `HEAD^1`. Feature deletions and renames are already resolved by the merge itself and are taken from the merged working state; patches changed by the target branch alone are not part of the transfer.
facts.REBASE-SCRATCH-TARGET-BASELINE: The target baseline is built in a scratch index and scratch objects from the patchset state at `HEAD^2`: its delta is applied onto its target pin, without the feature patches of the transferable set. Checking out a patchset ref, changing the refs of the tree and using already merged blobs for the baseline are forbidden. The feature patches from `HEAD^1` are applied onto that baseline one by one through PROP-008 §5; only after the full classification is the result carried into the working tree.
facts.REBASE-PIN-CAUSE-RULE: For `clean|shifted|merged|target-renamed` the patch is regenerated as the state "the target pin → the transferred file": every other header field is preserved, and `pin` becomes the exact `<tag>@<sha>` from `HEAD^2`. The old `cause` is preserved only for `clean` without a rename; for `shifted|merged|conflict|target-renamed|target-deleted` the cause of the change between the source and the target pin is computed per PROP-008 §7 (including `approx`; for `target-deleted` it stays in the red report until a human decides). For a conflict the target `pin/cause` are held in the local pending context of the operation and are written into the `.ckpatch` only together with the new body, by a subsequent `codkit save`; the intermediate pair "a new pin + an old body" is never written.
facts.REBASE-CONFLICT-RULE: Conflicts are materialized with the standard markers in the tree files over the scratch baseline of the target branch, and they are listed in full; after a manual resolution `codkit save` is run, and it finishes the pending regeneration. Codes: 0 - everything transferred cleanly; 1 - there are conflicts or broken feature artifacts; 2 - the merge or environment contract is violated.

p.CMD-CI: The container run "from scratch" (PROP-011). It always implies `--ci` (zero network). Profiles: `verify` (the default) - identity → a fresh bring-up to the pin → the apply → `verify` plus the race guards; `build` - the same plus the dependencies (the fast path), one compilation pass through the daemons, own tests and contract tests. Codes: 0; 1; 2.

p.CMD-CI-IMPL: The implementation after the post-M1 audit. The full signature: `ci [--profile verify|build] [--effective-diff <base-ref>] [--pin-guard-base <ref>] [--timeout <sec>]`; the command holds a per-tree lock for the whole run. The steps of verify (7 of them, printed in order with progress): the source of the path → the safe.directory probe (PROP-011 §5) → check-tree (in write mode) → a fresh load with the overlay targets materialized into the branch → verify → pin-guard (only with `--pin-guard-base`; otherwise the step is explicitly skipped) → effective-diff (only with the flag). Build runs 12 steps: the source → safe.directory → check-tree → a fresh load **without** the overlay targets → the dependencies → the real `npm run hygiene` and `npm run eslint` over the unmaterialized overlay → a second fresh load with overlay apply → verify → pin-guard → effective-diff → one pass of the daemons the type names (`build.defaultChannels`) → the real product/contract tests through `npm run test-node -- --runGlob vs/<ownDirName>/**/test/{common,node}/**/*.test.js` (the `common` and `node` layers of every `test/` directory under the own directory: the tests of the product, of the delivered library and of the feature directories; `--runGlob` goes around the standard exclusion of those layers by the node runner, while the suites of the `browser` layer run under the electron runner outside `ci` - PROP-010 §4). A red hygiene or test ends the command with code 1; a missing runner or script is code 2 `CK-E-LOG-INCOMPLETE`; there are no stubs that exit 0. The daemons are stopped in a finally block; an unfinished pass is `CK-E-LOG-INCOMPLETE`. Codes: 0; 1 - the checks, pin-guard, compilation or tests; 2 - the environment (`NET-FORBIDDEN`, `DEPS-MISSING`, a missing required runner). The step order is universal; the named scripts and globs are the project type's answer (VS Code type: `spec://codkit/modules/vscode/PROP-004#VSCODE-BUILD-STEPS`).

cmd-publish.title: 18. codkit publish patchset-ref [--profile verify|build] [--release semver] [--branch name] [--squash --author "Name <email>" --message-file path [--scrub]] --yes-i-am-publish-bot

p.CMD-PUBLISH: Build the generated branch from an immutable patchset commit and publish it into the fork. `patchset-ref` is required and is resolved once into a full commit SHA; `--profile verify|build` selects the checks and defaults to `verify`; `--release <semver>` additionally creates a release tag. The command requires a configured `publishRemoteUrl` and an explicit `--yes-i-am-publish-bot`; this is neither a human mode nor `--ci`: a `--ci` that is passed is rejected with code 2 `CK-E-NET-FORBIDDEN`, because publish has to reach the network. `--branch`, `--squash` and `--scrub` turn the release branch into a clean branch of the product source (`##PUBLISH-BRANCH-NAME`, `##PUBLISH-SQUASH`, `##PUBLISH-SCRUB`).

facts.PUBLISH-NETWORK-GATE: Before the fresh materialization and before any local or remote mutation, `git ls-remote <publishRemoteUrl>` is run; a failure → exit 2 naming the exact access required, with the tree and the refs unchanged. Only after the gate succeeds are the build and the push allowed; `publish` is the one codkit command where `netAllowed=true`, and only under the bot flag.
facts.PUBLISH-DISPOSABLE-FORK: The history is built and checked in a disposable fork, never in the caller's tree: the resolved patchset commit is checked out into a temporary snapshot, and the fork tree is cloned with `git clone --shared --no-checkout` into a temporary directory that the run removes whatever its outcome. The fork carries in its own config what codkit's git reads from no global or system config (PROP-002 `GIT-ENV-ISOLATION`): `core.longpaths=true`, because the fork lives deeper than the tree it copies and on Windows the longest upstream paths pass the 260-character limit otherwise (a no-op elsewhere); and, when git-lfs is installed and the tree has git-lfs content, the lfs filters that `git lfs install --local --skip-repo` writes - clean, smudge, process, required, and no hooks - with `lfs.storage` naming the lfs storage of the tree's common git directory, the way `--shared` shares its objects: the checkout of the pin smudges from local content, without the network. A tree without git-lfs or without lfs content is left alone, and check-tree names what is missing. The dependency roots of the project type are copied in as they are.
facts.PUBLISH-GENERATED-ORDER: The history is built from the pin in `codkit.json` at the resolved `patchset-ref`, strictly in this order: (1) the patch commits one by one, lexicographically by the UTF-8 path of the `.ckpatch`; (2) one own commit for the snapshot of `delta/own/**` when the own code being delivered is non-empty - minus `LICENSE-CODKIT.md`: the release branch does not carry the Codkit notice (PROP-014 §4a `STD-NOTICE-RELEASE-EXCLUSION`); an own snapshot made of that one notice is empty, and the commit is skipped; (3) the overlay commits by target, lexicographically by target, with the overlay composition of one target; (4) the resource commits by entries sorted by target. Then the selected profile of checks is run. Every one of these generated commits carries the canonical trailers with the exact case: `Codkit-Patchset-Commit: <the full 40-hex SHA of patchset-ref>` and `Codkit-Upstream-Pin: <pin.tag>@<the full 40-hex pin.sha>`.
facts.PUBLISH-REFS: Without `--branch` (`##PUBLISH-BRANCH-NAME`) the branch is named `codkit/release/<patchset12>+<pin.tag>`, where `patchset12` is exactly the first 12 lower-case hex characters of the resolved patchset SHA; the branch is pushed with `--force-with-lease`. With `--release <semver>` the local test contract, pending the owner's decision of PROP-012 §5, creates the tag `patchset-v<semver>+<pin.tag>` on the published tip: the generated tip, or the squashed commit under `--squash` (`##PUBLISH-SQUASH`). The tag is immutable: an absent one is published without force; one that already points at the same tip is an idempotent success; one that points at another tip is exit 1, with the tag neither moved nor deleted. An idempotent repeat after an interruption repeats only the pushes that were not delivered. Codes: 0; 1 - the checks or a conflict of the immutable tag; 2 - the network, the permissions or the environment.
facts.PUBLISH-BRANCH-NAME: `--branch <name>` names the published branch, for example `nimbus/rc/1.0.0`; without it the name is the one of `##PUBLISH-REFS`. The name is the short name of a branch: `refs/heads/<name>` must pass `git check-ref-format`, and a name that starts with `-` or `refs/`, or is `HEAD`, is refused. It must not collide with the namespaces of the patch set: a name inside `generatedBranchPrefix`, `cycleBranchPrefix` or `releaseRefPrefix` - of the `codkit.json` of the published commit or of the effective configuration - or a name that is a leading directory of one of them (`codkit` against `codkit/applied/`) is refused. Every refusal is exit 2 before the network gate. The lease, the repeat and the tag of `##PUBLISH-REFS` apply to the named branch unchanged.
facts.PUBLISH-SQUASH: `--squash` publishes one commit instead of the generated history. Its parent is `pin.sha`; its tree is exactly the tree of the tip the history of `##PUBLISH-GENERATED-ORDER` ends at - after `##PUBLISH-SCRUB` when `--scrub` is given as well. That history is still built in the disposable fork and the selected profile of checks runs over it unchanged; only the squashed commit leaves the fork. `--author "<Name> <email>"` is the author and the committer: a UTF-8 name, Cyrillic included, without `<`, `>` or a line break, and a non-empty address without spaces. `--message-file <path>` is the message: strict UTF-8 without a byte order mark and without NUL, CRLF read as LF, blank lines cut at both ends, one final LF; a message without text is refused. Both dates are the committer date of the patchset commit, so one patchset commit, author and message always make the same commit and a repeat is `up-to-date`. The squashed commit carries no Codkit trailer: its traceability is the release tag, which names it, and the message the owner writes. `--squash` without both `--author` and `--message-file`, and either of them without `--squash`, is exit 2 before the network gate, and so is an unreadable file or a malformed author. `data.squash` is `{parent, tree, unsquashedTip, author}`.
facts.PUBLISH-SCRUB: `--scrub` takes the tooling out of the release tree before the squashed commit is written; it needs `--squash` (a history that carries the markers is not clean), and alone it is exit 2. The delivered files are the regular files in which the unsquashed tip differs from the pin; nothing else is touched. In a delivered file that is strict UTF-8 the scrub removes: (a) every codkit marker line - a line that is only `<open>begin <name><close>` or `<open>end <name><close>` in any form of `markerComment` (PROP-004 §1: the shipped `// codkit:`, `/* codkit: … */`, `<!-- codkit: … -->`, `# codkit:` and the forms a conventions extension adds), where the name is an intervention id or the name of a managed block; (b) every `spec://` reference of a comment line: a parenthetical `(spec://…)` with its leading space - when it opens the text of the line, the punctuation right after it moves to the end of the previous comment line, if that line has text that does not end in punctuation already, and is dropped otherwise; a tag line whose only content is `@<tag> spec://…` (`@scope`, `@implements`, `@verifies` or any other tag); and a bare `spec://…` token, with its leading space; (c) the reference groups of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-GROUPS`, in comment text and in the prose of Markdown files. A comment line is a line whose first non-blank characters open a comment of the file's syntax, or that continues a block comment opened that way on an earlier line; the syntax is the one of the file's form in `markerComment`: `//` and `/* */` for the `//` form, `/* */` for the CSS form, `<!-- -->` for the markup form, `#` for the hash form. Text after the close of a block comment on the same line is code. A comment line the scrub leaves without text is dropped, except a line that opens or closes a block comment, which keeps its delimiters. Code lines, binary files and files whose extension has no form are never altered: what they carry is left to `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-FAIL-CLOSED`. Every changed file is reported with its counts - marker lines, spec references, reference groups, dropped lines - and so is every excluded file, the vocabulary by source and the groups removed by rule; `data.scrub` is `{files: [{path, markers, specRefs, droppedLines, groups: {parenthetical, lead, sentence, preposition}}], excluded, leftovers, vocabulary: {interventions, documents, stems, facts, modules, configured, allowed}}`. The runtime library under the own root stays (PROP-015 `RT-PUBLISH-KEEPS-THE-RUNTIME`): it is product code under its own licence header, and a build file that names its `codkit/` directory names a path, not a marker.
facts.PUBLISH-SCRUB-VOCABULARY: `--scrub` also takes out the bare references of the patch set - the ids it writes in prose without `spec://`. No naming pattern of any project is built in: the vocabulary is learned from the published commit and from the release. (1) The intervention ids: every id of the inventory of the published commit (PROP-006 `INVENTORY-IS-GENERATED`) and every name of a marker line of the delivered files; always on under `--scrub`. (2) The spec vocabulary, read from every `*.xml` file under the spec roots of the published commit, `publish.scrub.specRoots` (PROP-003 `CFG-PUBLISH-SCRUB-SPEC-ROOTS`), by default `vibevm/vibespecs`, where a vibevm project keeps its specifications - the layout Codkit already writes into for its standards (PROP-014 `STD-NOTICE-VIBE-COPIES` names the boot lane `vibevm/vibespecs/boot/` of the product). Of each document: its file stem (`FEAT-004-center-surfaces`); its document id, the longest part of the stem cut at a hyphen that the document's root title names as a word (`FEAT-004`, titled `nimbus FEAT-004: ...`); its fact ids, the names of the elements that carry `fact="true"` - which is how the spec dialect marks a fact - and the values of `id` attributes. Of every `spec://` reference in a delivered file: the last segment of its path, a stem or a short document id, and its fragment, a fact id. (3) The module names - the word of a root title before its document id (`nimbus`) and the first segment of a `spec://` path - are qualifiers only, never tokens. (4) `publish.scrub.vocabulary`: literal tokens and regular expressions the owner names for references that live elsewhere (`CFG-PUBLISH-SCRUB-VOCABULARY`). Every learned word passes `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-ID-SHAPE` first. The specmap is not a source: it is an index derived from the same documents, which a patch set need not carry - Nimbus carries none. A token matches case-sensitively where neither the character before it nor the one after it is a letter, a digit or `_`, the longest token first. A configured spec root that the published commit does not carry is a warning; an absent default root is silent. Measured on 2026-09-24 on the Nimbus replica: 156 intervention ids, 15 document ids, 15 stems, 582 fact ids and one module name.
facts.PUBLISH-SCRUB-ID-SHAPE: A learned word is a token only in the shape of an id: at least four characters, only letters, digits, `_`, `.` and `-`, opening and closing with a letter, a digit or `_`, with at least one upper-case letter and at least one hyphen or digit. The shape is read off the Nimbus data of 2026-09-24: every one of its 582 fact ids, 15 document ids and 156 intervention ids has an upper-case letter and a hyphen and is at least five characters long (the shortest are decisions such as `AP-D1`), while the generic words its sources yield lack one of these marks: `root`, the `id` of every root title, and the stem `WAL`. So do the names of the managed blocks a marker line may carry (`standards`, `components`, `scrape`) and the lower-case anchors and facts of codkit's own specifications (`config-valid-sample`). A project whose ids are lower case names them in `publish.scrub.vocabulary`, which the shape does not filter.
facts.PUBLISH-SCRUB-GROUPS: The bare references are removed as whole reference groups, in comment text - the comment lines of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB` - and in the prose of Markdown files (`.md`, `.markdown`): every line outside fenced code, an HTML comment being comment text. A group is a maximal run of tokens and their qualifiers: a token in backticks; a module name directly before a token (`nimbus FEAT-010`); `intervention` or `interventions` before an intervention id; `decision` before a token; after a token, `section <n>` and `decision <id>`, whose `<id>` has the shape of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-ID-SHAPE`; tokens joined by a comma, a semicolon, `and` or a blank. A group may continue onto the next line of the same comment paragraph or Markdown paragraph, and in Markdown prose a `spec://` reference is a token too. A group is removed in four places and only there: (1) a parenthetical that holds only the group, with the blank before it, also across lines - `(FEAT-007 CP-PROVIDERS)`, `(intervention `CK-build-002`)`, `(nimbus FEAT-010 AW-OWN-UNIT, AW-LOG)`, `(PROP-004` at the end of one line and `BU-D8)` on the next; (2) a group that opens a sentence and is followed by `:`, with the colon - `// FEAT-007 CP-PROVIDERS: a new chat` becomes `// a new chat`; (3) a sentence that is only the group, or `See`/`see` and the group - `See FEAT-005 `EP-SETTING`.`, `FEAT-006 `FR-TRIGGER`, `FR-GUARDS`.`; (4) a group after `of`, `in`, `by`, `per` or `from`, with the preposition - `the direction rule of FEAT-004 section 5b.` becomes `the direction rule.`, `Every rule of FEAT-004 section 5a that is about` becomes `Every rule that is about`. A sentence opens at the start of a paragraph or after `.`, `!` or `?` and a blank. Where something was removed, and only there, a blank before `.`, `,`, `:`, `;` or `)` goes, a double blank becomes one, a comma or a semicolon doubled across the gap becomes one, and a line whose start went gives its leading `.`, `,`, `;` or `:` to the end of the previous line of the paragraph when that line has text that does not end in punctuation, and drops it otherwise; a line left without text is dropped as `##PUBLISH-SCRUB` drops an emptied comment line. Every other occurrence stays in place for `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-FAIL-CLOSED` - prose the four places do not cover (`The owning specification is FEAT-004.`), a parenthetical with anything else in it, code and strings, data such as a JSON description, and a comment after code on the same line: code, fenced code and files that are neither commented nor Markdown are never altered. Measured on 2026-09-24 on the Nimbus replica: 125 parentheticals, 11 groups with a colon, 13 sentences and 12 groups after a preposition, in 112 files.
facts.PUBLISH-EXCLUDE: `publish.exclude` names paths of the release tree, a file or a directory, that `--scrub` leaves out of the release: the list of the `codkit.json` of the published commit joined with the list of `codkit.local.json` (PROP-003 `CFG-PUBLISH-EXCLUDE`). A delivered file the pin does not carry is left out of the tree. An entry that names a path the pin carries is exit 2 before the network gate - an exclusion leaves out what the patch set adds and never deletes or reverts upstream's bytes; an entry that matches no delivered file is a warning.
facts.PUBLISH-SCRUB-FAIL-CLOSED: After the scrub and the exclusions the whole release tree is searched for `codkit:begin`, `codkit:end`, `spec://` and `vibevm` - the last one names the spec tooling, which is not part of the product - ignoring case, binary files included. Any hit stops the publish before the first remote write: exit 1, `data.status` `scrub-failed`, one `CK-E-CONFIG` error per hit naming the file and the line (a binary file has no line), and nothing is pushed. Every delivered file left in the tree is searched as well for the vocabulary of `##PUBLISH-SCRUB-VOCABULARY` - a text file line by line, a binary file as its bytes - with the matching of that fact: a line that still carries a token stops the publish the same way, and its error names the tokens; a line the first search already names is named once. The files the pin carries unchanged are upstream's bytes, never a reference of the patch set, and are not searched for vocabulary. A leftover of `data.scrub.leftovers` is `{path, line, text, tokens}`, with `tokens` empty for a hit of the first search. The way out is the owner's: an exclusion, a change of the file in the patch set, or - for a token the release may carry where the scrub leaves it - `publish.scrub.allow` (PROP-003 `CFG-PUBLISH-SCRUB-ALLOW`): the search lets an allowed token through, and the scrub still takes out every group it is in.
facts.PUBLISH-LOCAL-REMOTE: `publishRemoteUrl` may be a local path set in `codkit.local.json`, bare repository or not: the `ls-remote` gate, the lease and the pushes run against it as against a hosted fork. A repository with a working tree takes a push to any branch but the one it has checked out. Measured on 2026-09-24: the e2e fixture publishes into a local bare remote, and a replica of Nimbus published its clean release branch into a bare clone of the upstream repository.

p.CMD-HOOKS: `install`: it installs (a) a `commit-msg` hook in patchset: when `cycle/state.json` exists it appends the trailer `Codkit-Cycle: <targetTag>`, and it checks the format of the `Cause:` trailer when one is present; (b) a `pre-commit` hook in patchset: a fast check of the markers and of the schemas of the changed `delta/**` files (fractions of a second per file). Success of `install`/`check` means not only the exact owned bytes but proof that the real Git executes exactly this path: the effective `--git-path hooks/<name>` is resolved across every local/global/system scope and compared canonically (on Windows: slash and case semantics). A linked worktree (the hooks are shared), any custom `core.hooksPath`, `/dev/null`, a failed resolution and a foreign hook are an explicit inactive/refusal; Codkit does not write implicitly into a shared, global or foreign location. `check` is green only for effective and current owned bytes. CI checks the trailers independently. The hook of the tree is PROP-012 §5 and has the same linked/custom/foreign exceptions.

p.CMD-GC: Remove the spent runtime state of patchset; the closed list of classes is PROP-006 §1 `##GC-CLASSES` (the TREE-COMMITS-SAVE campaign, Phase 9, decision D22). Order: the tree lock → the plan → the removal. The plan prints every candidate with its class and its remove/keep action - the kept classes included, with an explanation (the transaction of a stopped `sync`, the pending drafts, the daemon records, the lock of a live owner with its pid and command): the plan is what the operator reviews, not merely a list of removals. A stale lock of **its own** tree is lifted by the acquisition itself (as always, PROP-006 §2), and gc names that lifting in the plan; locks of foreign trees with a dead pid are lifted by gc through the same acquisition protocol, and with a live pid it keeps them. It removes: `refs/codkit/consumed/*` older than `--older-than` days (default 30) beyond the last `--keep-consumed` (default 5; the refs are shared by every worktree - the removal happens under the lock of the shared repository), `.codkit/tmp/*`, the cache `.codkit/trees/<id>.json` of a tree that does not exist, and `.codkit/out/*`. Never: the transactions, the receipts and pending, `.codkit/build/*`, the `daemon-*` locks, and the git objects of the tree. `--dry-run` is the same plan without the removal; the actual removal must match the printed plan one for one (R14). `--json`: `data.plan`, `data.removed`, `data.kept`. Codes: 0; 2 (the environment; an invalid `--keep-consumed`/`--older-than` is a refusal before any lock).

p.CMD-IMAGESET: `codkit imageset gen [--dry-run] [--branding-dir path]` regenerates the product's icon set from the branding masters; it is delivered by the resource-file layer (PROP-005 §6): the files land in `delta/resources/files/`, the entries in `delta/resources/map.json`, and an ordinary `load` materializes them - the product repository receives resource artifacts indistinguishable from hand-made ones, with no trace of how they were produced. Only the operator runs the command (the namespace is `##IMAGESET-NAMESPACE`): no codkit command calls it and it calls nothing that mutates; a human reviews and commits the patchset diff. Preconditions: the config (the map entries carry the pin `tag@sha`), the fork tree exists (the targets are read from it). The first run, when the masters directory is absent, creates it and fills it with the icons of the distribution itself from the tree (seeding, `##IMAGESET-MASTERS`) - with a report; an existing directory is never overwritten. A new map entry requires a guard test `guard.brand.<family>` declared under own beforehand (`CK-E-GUARD-MISSING`, a refusal BEFORE the first write - the resource layer has no markers, so the guard is mandatory) and an owner: the first key of `delta/owners.json` whose paths cover the target (with nothing covering it - `CK-E-OWNER-UNKNOWN`); for an existing entry only the bytes of its source and the pin are updated. `--dry-run` is the same plan (the seeding, the targets, the frames, the origin of every frame, the entries) without a single write, and it reads every master the run would read, so it refuses and skips as the run does (`##IMAGESET-SELF-CHECK-READS-MASTERS`). A target without a family master is a warning and exit 1. `--help` lives on the namespace and prints the long help BEFORE the roots are resolved (`##IMAGESET-NO-TOOLS`). `--json`: `data.brandingDir`, `data.seeded`, `data.targets[]` (the frames, each with where it came from - `##IMAGESET-FRAME-SOURCES-REPORTED` - `skipped`, `entry`, `legacyTypes`), `data.written`. What the shipped files cannot say - the frame set of a target, the master key of some of its frames - the product declares in its masters directory (`##IMAGESET-DECLARATION`). Codes: 0; 1 (there are skipped targets); 2 (the environment: no tree, a broken target container, no guard or owner, no native rasterizer).

p.IMAGESET-TARGET-DISCOVERY: Tombstone (PROP-016 split, 2026-09-09): moved to spec://codkit/modules/vscode/PROP-006#IMAGESET-TARGET-DISCOVERY; the address stays for citations.

p.IMAGESET-MASTERS: The masters live by default in `<patchset>/branding/` - a derivative of the root of the product repository; `--branding-dir` exists only to override that, and a run without the flag has to work. The naming convention, where `<key>` is the family for a family holding one drawing and `<family>/<artwork>` for one holding several (`##IMAGESET-ARTWORK`): `<key>.svg` is a vector master (rendered at every size, preferred), `<key>.png` a raster one (resampling), `<key>-<N>.png` an override for the NxN size, `<key>-<W>x<H>.png` one for the non-square sizes; an override is used verbatim and has to match the size of the frame, otherwise the target is honestly skipped. Precedence: an override > svg > png - the operator generates the small sizes with external tools and puts them alongside, and masters of the exact size beat generated reductions. A file that fits no convention is printed as ignored - nothing is picked up or skipped silently; the walk of the directory is recursive, because the subdirectories of the families are part of the convention and not stray folders. The declaration of the image set, `imageset.json` in the root of the directory (`##IMAGESET-DECLARATION`), is recognised as well - it is not a master - and so is every master of a key a rule of it names: neither is ever reported as ignored. Seeding: when the directory is absent it is created and filled with the distribution's own artwork - for every key the largest raster among ITS OWN targets is taken and placed as `<key>.png`, and for a vector family the vector itself is placed as `<key>.svg`. A container codkit can only write and not read (the ICO frames, the XPM palette) contributes nothing to the seeding - which is why the `icon` family is seeded from the PNG and ICNS targets the same family carries, and not from the `.ico`. The seeding is always printed; an existing directory is never overwritten.

p.IMAGESET-CONTAINERS: The container codecs are hand-written, with no image dependencies: ICO - a 6-byte header plus 16 bytes per directory frame, PNG payloads (legal since Vista), a size byte of 0 meaning 256; ICNS - `icns` plus the total length, elements of `<type><length including the header><PNG>`; the BMP of the installer graphics - 24 bits without alpha, the background written explicitly (white), rows bottom-up aligned to 4; XPM - the XPM3 form `static char * …_xpm[]`, the palette from a histogram of the exact colors (flat artwork keeps a small palette) with a median cut on overflow, 1–2 characters per pixel, transparency as the color `None`; PNG - a codec of our own (decoding: which variants are read and what a refused file is told is `##IMAGESET-PNG-MASTERS`; encoding is deterministic: filter 0, a fixed deflate level - a repeated regeneration gives an empty diff).

p.IMAGESET-PNG-MASTERS: A PNG master is read in every variant the PNG format defines, because whatever a designer's tool exports has to be usable as it is, without a conversion by hand: grey at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 bits; RGB, grey with alpha and RGBA at 8 and 16 bits; a palette at 1, 2, 4 and 8 bits; a `tRNS` chunk in each - an alpha for every palette entry, and for grey and RGB the one colour, compared sample by sample at the depth of the file, that is transparent; and Adam7 interlacing. The pipeline works in 8 bits per channel (`##IMAGESET-RASTER`, `##IMAGESET-CONTAINERS`), so a 16-bit sample is brought to 8 bits by rounding, value8 = round(value16 × 255 / 65535) - the nearest of the 256 levels, exact at both ends because 65535 = 255 × 257 - and a grey sample of 1, 2 or 4 bits is scaled to the full range, value × 255 / (2^depth − 1). The samples are taken as stored: no gamma or colour-space chunk is applied. Only a file that is not a well-formed PNG is refused - no signature, no intact IHDR, a colour type or a depth the format does not define (RGB at 4 bits, for instance), a compression, filter or interlace method it does not define, a palette image without PLTE, image data that does not inflate or does not fill the passes its header declares, a scanline filter it does not define - and the refusal says what is wrong with the file and what to export instead: an 8-bit RGBA PNG. It stays `CK-E-ARTIFACT-BROKEN` naming the master, the one refusal the contract carries (`spec://codkit/modules/codkit/PROP-016#TYPE-API-STABILITY`); a precise message, not a new code, is what the operator needs to act on.

p.IMAGESET-RASTER: The raster path is only for raster masters and mismatched aspects: a separable Lanczos-3 over premultiplied alpha with normalized weights and clamps (ringing must not wrap the alpha modulo 256); the vector path does not resample at all - every size is rendered by the rasterizer at its native resolution. The quantization of the XPM palette is in `##IMAGESET-CONTAINERS`. The candidate dependency `sharp` is excluded by the licence rule (libvips is LGPL) without discussion.

p.IMAGESET-RENDER: Rasterization is `@resvg/resvg-js` 2.6.2 (MPL-2.0), the only dependency of the command: twelve prebuilt platform binaries (darwin x64/arm64, linux x64/arm64/arm in gnu and musl, win32 x64/ia32/arm64, android), and nothing is installed onto the host. The native module is loaded lazily - the other commands do not pay for it and do not fall over a platform binary that is not theirs; a missing module is `CK-E-DEPS-MISSING`. When the aspect of the master does not match the target: render by width, then resample to the exact sizes.

p.IMAGESET-STRETCH-REPORTED:
When the aspect of a vector master differs from the aspect of a raster frame it renders, the frame is still produced at the exact size (`##IMAGESET-RENDER` renders by width, `##IMAGESET-RASTER` resamples to the exact height), but the drawing loses its proportions - a fact of the design whoever draws has to see - so every report of that frame says it is stretched and by how much. **The measure** is one for every report: with the intrinsic size of the master `w`x`h` and the frame `W`x`H`, the stretch is |H·w / (W·h) − 1|, how far the height of the frame departs from the height the master's own aspect gives it at the width of the frame, as a percentage rounded to one decimal; a frame is stretched when that figure is at least 0.1%. A 400x800 master comes out of the rasteriser at 164x328 for a 164x314 frame and is stretched 4.3%. **The wording** is one as well: the origin of the frame in `gen` and `gen --dry-run` reads `rendered at x, stretched

% from the master's aspect`, and the From column of `index` reads `rendered at this size from , stretched

% from the master's aspect`. Both runs of `gen` also print one warning line per stretched frame through the ordinary warning channel, naming the target and the master's own size; the exit code does not change, because the frame is delivered. **The fields:** under `--json` every frame of `data.targets[].frames[]` (`gen`) and every size of `data.targets[].sizes[]` (`index`) carries `stretched` and `stretchPercent`. A frame no vector master renders is not assessed and carries `stretched: false` and `stretchPercent: null`: a per-size override is used at exactly its own size, a raster master already reports `resampled`, and a vector target is emitted unchanged at the size it has to carry (`##IMAGESET-SVG-PASSTHROUGH`). **The prediction** of `gen --dry-run` and `index` renders nothing and still cannot disagree with the run, because the intrinsic size is the rasteriser's own reading of the master the run would render - in a dry run that plans the seeding, the bytes the seeding would write: `@resvg/resvg-js` parses it as the render does - the render only adds the fit to the width of the frame, which sizes the output and leaves the parse alone - and, without rendering, gives the size of its tree on the root element of `Resvg#toString()`; the run reads the same root off the instance that rendered the frame. The `Resvg#width` and `Resvg#height` getters are not used, because they round that size to whole pixels - a 32.5x65 master reads as 33x65 there and would report 1.5% at a 164x328 frame the render fills exactly - and no second reader of the document is used either, because usvg resolves units, percentages and a missing `height` by rules of its own: `width="200"` with the viewBox `0 0 400 800` and no `height` is a 200x800 drawing to it.

p.IMAGESET-SELF-CHECK-READS-MASTERS: `gen --dry-run` and `index` are the self-check a designer runs before the real `gen`, so neither may promise a run that then fails: each reads every master the run would read, with the code the run reads it with, and says what the run would say. **What is read** is what the run reads, in its order: target by target and frame by frame, the master the run chooses for the frame (`##IMAGESET-MASTERS`) - in a dry run that plans the seeding, the bytes the seeding would write - and a target is read no further than the frame the run gives it up at, so a file the run never opens cannot fail the check; a size of `index` past that frame is neither assessed for a stretch nor reported as reduced. **A PNG master**, a per-size override or `<key>.png`, is decoded in full by the run's decoder (`##IMAGESET-PNG-MASTERS`). A file the run refuses is refused with the same `CK-E-ARTIFACT-BROKEN`, message and hint, exit 2 - by `index` too, because an index that listed the master would describe a run that does not happen. An override whose decoded size is not the size of its frame gets the run's own skip: in the dry run the warning `skipped <target>: the per-size override <file> does not cover <W>x<H>` and exit 1, in `index` the same reason in the From column of that size. **The master of a vector target** is parsed and its size compared as the run does (`##IMAGESET-SVG-PASSTHROUGH`): whatever makes the run skip the target - a master that is not a vector, does not parse or has another size - is the same skip, with the same reason, in both. **A vector master** is read for its stretch (`##IMAGESET-STRETCH-REPORTED`), which already refuses one the rasteriser cannot parse. **A 16-bit master** is reported as reduced to 8 bits, because that is a fact of the file the designer delivered: the origin of every frame it serves ends in `, reduced from 16 to 8 bits per channel` in `gen` and `gen --dry-run`, the From column of `index` ends in the same words, and under `--json` every frame of `gen` and every size of `index` carries `reducedFrom16Bit`. It is not a warning - the delivered images carry 8 bits per channel whatever the master holds - and a master of fewer bits, expanded to 8 without a loss, is not reported. Under `--json` every target of `index` also carries `skipped`: the reason the run skips it, in the words of the run's warning, or null. Only the pixels are left out: the check resamples, renders and encodes nothing.

p.IMAGESET-DECLARATION: **The product declares what its shipped files cannot say, in one data file next to the masters it names** (`##DECISION-IMAGESET-DECLARATION-FILE`). The file is `imageset.json` in the root of the masters directory - `<patchset>/branding/imageset.json`, or the root of the directory `--branding-dir` names - and it is versioned with the masters in the product repository; without it nothing changes. Version 1 is an object `{"codkitImageset": 1, "targets": {…}}` whose `targets` maps a target, named by its path in the fork tree with forward slashes exactly as `codkit imageset index` prints it, to an entry with `frames`, the frame set of the target (`##IMAGESET-DECLARED-FRAMES`), and `sources`, the rules that give some of its frames to another master key (`##IMAGESET-DECLARED-SOURCES`); an entry carries at least one of the two. The complete declaration of the case it was made for: `{"codkitImageset": 1, "targets": {"resources/win32/code.ico": {"frames": [16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 128, 256], "sources": [{"key": "taskbar", "maxSize": 64}]}}}` - nine frames in place of the four the pin ships, those up to 64 px from the masters of the key `taskbar` and the larger ones from the target's own key `icon`, with `resources/server/favicon.ico` and the rest of the family untouched. `gen`, `gen --dry-run`, `index` and `verify` read the file and validate all of it before they read a master or write a byte, and every problem is `CK-E-CONFIG`, exit 2, naming the file, the target and the rule: a file that is not a JSON object, a `codkitImageset` other than 1, a member version 1 does not define at any level, a target path that is not a target of the distribution, an entry that declares nothing, and each problem the two facts below name. A declaration is applied exactly or refused: nothing in it is ignored, applied in part or replaced by a fallback.
